name: Gemini 6A / GT-6A
dispatch: Rendezvous — two spacecraft finding and joining each other in orbit — was the skill Apollo could not do without, and Gemini 6A is where it was first done. It nearly didn't fly: its original target blew up on the way to orbit, and then, strapped in for the rescheduled launch, the Titan's engines lit and abruptly died on the pad — a moment when the rules said eject, and Wally Schirra, feeling no motion, coolly chose not to. Three days later it flew and did the thing that had never been done: caught up with Gemini 7 and held station a foot away, the crews close enough to read each other's faces. It looked easy and was anything but — the orbital mechanics of catching another craft are deeply counter-intuitive — and cracking it was the moment lunar-orbit rendezvous, and the whole Apollo plan, became real.
description: Wally Schirra and Tom Stafford achieved the first crewed space rendezvous on 15 December 1965, station-keeping within ~30 cm of Gemini 7 for over five hours. It followed a launch-pad engine shutdown three days earlier that Schirra chose not to abort. Duration ~1 d 1 h; 16 orbits.

events.label: PAD SHUTDOWN
events.note: 1965-12-12: engines ignite then shut down on the pad; Schirra does not eject.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Titan II GLV (GT-6A) from Cape Canaveral LC-19, 1965-12-15 13:37 UTC.

events.label: RENDEZVOUS
events.note: First crewed rendezvous — station-keeps within ~30 cm of Gemini 7.

events.label: SPLASHDOWN
events.note: Atlantic splashdown after ~1 d 1 h / 16 orbits.
